Tyhra

Tyhra

Orrondar – The center of order

At the heart of the continent lay Orrondar a well-ordered land, crisscrossed by roads, fields, and cities where all peoples had once been represented equally. From above, it appeared like a finely drawn pattern: geometric, clear, symmetrical. Thyrros, the god of truth and law, was revered there. His paladins and judges safeguarded justice and the well-being of the community. After the War of the Gods, Orrondar became the model for what the Eight called safety through order.
The gods had issued the Sentinel Mandate holy detachments dispatched into towns and even remote villages, tasked with guarding the people against the lingering monsters of the old world. Truth be told, such creatures had grown rarer with every passing decade.
Yet they remained common enough in rumor and real enough in the deep woods and forgotten grottos that fear never fully left the hearthfires.
The Sentinels were the answer the gods provided: protection, patrol, and the comforting weight of authority at every gate. Equilara, also known as “The City of Law,” served as the center of justice and communal life in Orrondar a place where the values of Thyrros were deeply woven into both architecture and daily life. The city lay at the confluence of two rivers, known as the River of Clarity and the River of Protection, symbolizing the core principles of Orrondarian society: transparency and care. All buildings in Equilara had been arranged symmetrically, and the city was divided into meticulously planned districts, each serving the greater purpose of harmony and structured coexistence. At the heart of the city stood the Temple of Truth, a grand structure of pale stone that housed the High Court and the Council of Paladins. The temple was adorned with symbols of Thyrros’ protection and wisdom and contained the Great Scale a ceremonial artifact representing the balance of truth and justice. It was overseen by the priests and paladins of Thyrros, known as the “Guardians of Truth,” who had been devoted to upholding the law with fairness and shielding society from deceit and injustice.

Athera – The living cycle

To the west lay Athera, a land of rolling hills, roaring coasts, and fire-spewing mountains. Halflings and humans had been the dominant peoples there, though elves and dwarves had also called this land home. The region was both fertile and perilous shaped by constant change. It was there that Thronos, the Warden of the Natural Cycle, had been worshipped. His signs had manifested in animal traits and in the whispering of the woods.

Silverspring served as the capital of Athera, located on the banks of the emerald green Beryllus River. The city had been famed for its silver mines and the exceptional craftsmanship of its smiths. Surrounded by fertile fields and dense forests, Silverspring had been both protected by and dependent upon its natural surroundings vital for both defense and agriculture.

Velenor

South of Athera lay Velenor, a land infused with magic, like a tapestry woven from the Six Constant Stars.
Its capital, Astralan, sat atop a high plateau. Humans and centaurs dwelled there, living in close communion with Azarath, the goddess of time and fate.
They read the threads of the future in the Constants, in woven rugs, and in prophetic visions.

Astralan was perched upon a plateau from which one could gaze across the vast sweep of darkness, pierced by the Six.
Often called the “City of Stars,” it was regarded as the spiritual heart of Velenor.
In Astralan, every aspect of life seemed to revolve around the heavens and the mysteries of destiny.
Symbols of Azarath were found throughout the city: all-seeing eyes representing omniscience, and intricate star patterns adorning the facades of homes and temples alike.

At the city’s heart stood the Temple of the Infinite Weave, a monumental structure built from polished, silver-hued stone that seemed to glow beneath moonlight.
The temple was aligned with the brightest Constant, known as the “Eye of Azarath.”
Inside, a massive wall tapestry depicted the fabric of fate — a masterpiece of golden and silver threads that appeared to shimmer and shift with the changing light.
It was said that the temple’s high priests could read the future, and the fate-threads of every soul, within this living tapestry.

Astravar

Directly to the east lay Astravar a tranquil land of knowledge and compassion. Centaurs and humans had lived in white cities filled with healing gardens and libraries. Valkath, goddess of magic and healing, had been worshipped there. Her light had brought hope, wisdom, and restoration manifesting through the sacred rituals of the “Enlightened.”

Illumara, also known as “The City of the Sacred Flame,” had been the heart of Astravar and a center for the study and practice of healing arts and magic. The city rested upon a gentle plateau and had been known for its white stone buildings, which gleamed in the sunlight and were adorned with healing symbols and arcane runes. The streets of Illumara had been spacious and paved with mosaics depicting Valkath’s symbols healing hands, crystals, and radiant flames representing the flow of magical and restorative energy.

At the center of the city stood the Temple of Enlightenment, a magnificent structure crowned by a great glass dome that captured the sunlight and scattered it across the city in vibrant colors. Within the temple burned Valkath’s Heart, an eternal flame revered as a sacred symbol of the goddess’s healing power and arcane wisdom. The temple’s priests and priestesses known as the “Keepers of the Flame” had tended to the fire and offered healing rituals and blessings to all who had sought comfort or protection. The flame had been considered a living manifestation of Valkath’s blessing and had drawn pilgrims from across the world, seeking both spiritual and physical healing within its radiant glow.

Zehrion

In the southeast lay the vast, desert-like expanse of Zehrion. Storms had raced across its skies, and though the land had been dry, it had not been lifeless. Nomadic centaurs and minotaurs had roamed the plains with tents and feathers, following the wind. Their goddess had been Sylphoria, the deity of freedom, who had spoken through the breeze. There had been no permanent cities there only wandering gatherings such as Aerithar.

The capital of Zehrion had not been a traditional city of buildings and streets. Known as Aerithar, it had been a temporary, traveling city assembled by the clans once each year for the Great Wind Ceremony. Its exact location had shifted from year to year, determined by the signs of the wind and the interpretations of tribal leaders, who had read the skies and weather to divine the place of gathering.

During the Wind Ceremony, Aerithar had transformed into a vibrant, pulsing city of tents, banners, and colorful cloth dancing in the wind. The tents had been elaborately painted and decorated with Sylphoria’s symbols spirals representing the eternal cycle of life and change. A festive atmosphere had filled the air as tribes had exchanged stories, traded goods, and held competitions celebrating physical prowess and spiritual insight. It had been a time of sharing and the renewal of bonds between clans.

At the heart of Aerithar had stood the Altar of Winds, a simple yet sacred structure made of stones and feathers — the holiest site in Zehrion’s culture. The altar had been erected for the Wind Ceremony and had served as a place of offering to Sylphoria. Tribal leaders had gathered there to present prayers and gifts, seeking the goddess’s guidance. It was said that when the prayers had been sincere, a warm wind had stirred across the altar, lifting the feathers into the air — a sign of Sylphoria’s blessing.

Karaveth

Northeast of Zehrion lay Karaveth, a bustling realm of deception, secrets, and gold. Merchants, spies, and diplomats primarily dwarves and humans had traversed this hilly land filled with vibrant bazaars and secret auctions. Ithkor, god of trade and trickery, had been worshipped there. His masks, coins, and rituals had been woven into every deal struck and every promise made.

The capital city, Draemir, had been the beating heart of Karaveth’s commerce a labyrinth of secrets and ambition. Draemir had been famed for its maze-like markets and alleys, where one could have found every kind of good from fine silks and exotic spices to rare artifacts and hidden knowledge. Built upon the ruins of an ancient trade city, many of Draemir’s buildings had contained underground chambers and secret passages used by smugglers and merchants alike. Here, in the shadows of its narrow streets, trade had thrived not only in goods, but in whispers and confidential exchanges.

At the center of Draemir had risen the Obsidian Tower of Ithkor, an imposing structure of dark stone that had served as both the religious and economic heart of the city. The tower had housed the Guild of Ithkor, a powerful organization that had controlled the flow of goods and information across Karaveth. Composed of seasoned traders, spies, and diplomats, the guild had adhered to Ithkor’s teachings and had excelled in the arts of deception and manipulation. The tower had also contained a vast archive of valuable trade agreements, secret contracts, and intelligence on the continent’s most influential merchants and political leaders — knowledge the guild had wielded with precision and cunning.

The Grand Bazaar had been the center of daily life in Draemir a vast, covered market where merchants from every corner of the world had sold their wares. There, visitors could have found rare and exotic goods, and it had been an open secret that more illicit dealings had taken place in the shadowy backstreets. Contracts had been sealed in hushed corners over a glass of wine, and it had not been uncommon for the most profitable negotiations to revolve not around price, but information. One tradition had endured above all others: every new merchant had tossed a coin into the Bazaar’s Fountain and had whispered a small secret to Ithkor, hoping to earn his favor.

Kalgrad

Far to the north rose Kalgrad, a harsh land of icy mountains, volcanic craters, and blazing forges. Minotaurs and dwarves had defied the cold there. Xaldris, goddess of war and smithing, had been their flame in the storm. Fortresses, anvils, and trials by fire had shaped both body and spirit.

The capital of Kalgrad had been Kaldrheim, also known as “The City of Embers.” Built upon a volcanic plateau, Kaldrheim had drawn warmth and energy from the magma beneath the frozen surface. This underground heat had sustained the city, but the Kalgradi had used it sparingly, in accordance with their disciplined way of life. The buildings had been constructed of black basalt and metal, built to withstand the harshest weather. Kaldrheim had stood as a fortress of resolve and discipline, and every aspect from its simple, sturdy structures to its ever-burning hearths, had reflected the warrior culture of its people.

At the city’s heart had stood the Flame Temple of Xaldris, an imposing structure that had housed an eternal flame. This sacred fire had been guarded by the Blades of Flame, priest-warriors who had undergone both physical and spiritual trials to become its keepers. They had forged weapons and armor in the temple’s sacred fire and had trained to uphold Xaldris’ honor and will in battle. The Flame Temple had served not only as a place of worship, but also as a warrior academy, where the Blades of Flame had prepared the next generation.

Once each year, Kaldrheim had hosted the Trial of Embers, a sacred rite in which young Kalgradi warriors had proven their strength and devotion to Xaldris. Aspirants had plunged into icy waters before grasping a glowing weapon and swearing an oath to the goddess. Only those who had endured the trial had been granted the title of Blade of Flame and had earned the right to enter the temple and guard the eternal flame.

Morrdrak

In the far west lay Morrdrak, a quiet, mist-shrouded land of swamps, rivers, and shadows. Titanborn and humans had walked there between life and death. Nethrion, god of gentle farewells, had guided the souls of the departed through rivers and dreams. Lanterns on the water and silence had marked this melancholic, reverent realm.

Nimrath, also known as “The City of Shadows,” had been Morrdrak’s spiritual heart, perched on a hill above the vast moorlands. Its buildings, made of dark stone, had been overgrown with moss and lichen, lending them a timeworn beauty. The streets had been narrow and winding, and at night only a few lanterns had burned, their dim, flickering light casting shadows that had seemed to whisper as they shone through the alleys. A deep and peaceful stillness had pervaded the city, which the people had honored quietly, as if unwilling to disturb the dead who might still have wandered its streets.

The Black Temple of Nethrion, the imposing heart of Nimrath, had been built from black basalt and had risen with tall, slender spires. The temple had served as a place of remembrance and preparation for the final journey. Nethrion’s priests, known as the Shadow Wardens, had performed rituals there to release souls into peace and rest. The temple had also been a center for the “Art of Letting Go,” a spiritual practice that had helped the living heal grief and old wounds, while allowing the dead to depart with compassion. The Shadow Wardens had taught that letting go and accepting death had been a gift of Nethrion — one that had brought peace and solace to all who embraced it.
